sections.title: Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) Risk Factors

branches: Race: Black people 4 times > white people

sections.title: Anderson's Criteria & AGIS Insights
content: Minimal criteria for glaucoma damage on SAP (Anderson’s criteria):
1. GHT (Glaucoma Hemifield Test): Outside normal level at least 2 occasions.
2. Cluster of three or more non-edge points in a location typical for glaucoma, all of which are depressed on PSD at <5% and one which is depressed at p<1% level on two consecutive occasions.
3. Corrected PSD that occurs in less than 5% of normal individuals on two consecutive occasions.
AGIS (Advanced Glaucoma Interventional Study): Significant visual field progression is unlikely to occur in most patients in the medium term if IOP can be kept below 18mmHg at all times.

branches: Systemic hypotension: Nocturnal dip in BP >20% (especially on oral hypotensives)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Normal Tension Glaucoma

rows: Angle closure glaucoma; Falsely low IOP (ectasia, LASIK); Myopic degeneration; Optic disc drusen; Congenital disc anomalies
POAG + normal IOP due to diurnal fluctuation; Previous episodes of raised IOP (trauma, uveitis, steroid therapy); Masked by systemic beta-blockers
Neurological lesion; Previous AION secondary to Temporal Arteritis; Previous acute optic nerve insult; Miscellaneous optic nerve neuropathy

sections.title: Primary Angle Closure (PAC) Classification
content: 1. Primary Angle Closure Suspect (PACS): ACD < normal. Gonioscopy: ITC in >= 3 quadrants, no PAS. OR 2 quadrants of ITC + signs of intermittent closure (pigment smudging). Normal IOP, optic disc, and visual field.
2. Primary Angle Closure (PAC): Gonioscopy: >= 3 quadrants of ITC + raised IOP and/or PAS. Normal optic disc and field. Ischaemic PAC shows iris changes and Glaukomflecken.
3. Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (PACG): Gonioscopy: ITC in >= 3 quadrants + Glaucomatous Optic Neuropathy.

sections.title: PACG Risk Factors & Definitions
content: Lens Vault Definition: The distance between the anterior pole of the lens and a horizontal line joining scleral spurs at diametrically opposite locations.
Age: Pupillary block (~62y); Non-pupillary block (younger).
Gender: Female predominance.
Race: Non-pupillary block prevalent in Far Eastern and Indian Asians.
Family History: Poorly defined but increased prevalence in family members.
Refraction: Pupillary block (Hypermetropes); Non-pupillary block (can occur in Myopes).
Axial Length: Short eyes tend to have a shallow AC (Anterior Chamber).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute IOP Elevation
content: Lens-induced angle closure (swollen/subluxated lens)
Malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection - post-op)
Secondary angle closure (with/without pupillary block)
Neovascular glaucoma (sudden pain/congestion)
Hypertensive uveitis (Iridocyclitis, Trabeculitis, CMV, Posner-Schlossman)
Scleritis (with/without angle closure)
Pigment dispersion
Pseudoexfoliation
Orbital/Retrobulbar lesions (Inflammation, Hemorrhage, CC-Fistula)

sections.title: Pseudoexfoliation (PXS) & Systemic Health
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation material is a grey-white fibrillary substance derived from abnormal extracellular matrix metabolism in ocular and other tissues. Systemic manifestations include: 1. High-tone hearing loss. 2. Ischaemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. 3. Increased risk of pelvic organ prolapse in older women.

rows: Factors for poor outcome: Young age, VA < 6/60, IOP > 35mmHg
Established glaucoma/OHT; +ve FH; High Myopia; Young age (childhood); Connective tissue disease (RA)

content.explanation: 1. Total hyphema. 2. IOP > 50mmHg for 2 days. 3. IOP > 35mmHg for 5 days.
